hook.text: Design a fraud detection system. That's the classic machine learning system design prompt.

hook-now.text: Now it's just as often: design an assistant over our documents. Or: this LLM feature is too slow and too expensive. Fix it.

hook-both.text: These videos cover both kinds: what every ML round still asks, and what large language models, LLMs, added.

rounds.text: Expect three rounds: coding, ML concepts, and ML system design. Across them, interviewers probe four areas.

rounds-probe.text: ML fundamentals: supervised and unsupervised learning, over- and underfitting, regularization, metrics and leakage. Coding: data structures and algorithms, plus NumPy and pandas.

rounds-ops.text: System design: training and serving pipelines, feature stores, batch or online inference, monitoring and drift. And MLOps: reproducibility, versioning data and models, CI CD, latency and cost.
rounds-ops.spoken: System design: training and serving pipelines, feature stores, batch or online inference, monitoring and drift. And em-el-ops: reproducibility, versioning data and models, CI CD, latency and cost.

rounds-more.text: The track adds pages on statistics, deep learning, and NLP and LLMs, and each of those gets a part too.

llm.text: Classical ML didn't leave when LLMs arrived: bias and variance, leakage, metrics and a coding round are all still asked. What LLMs added is four things.

llm-design.text: Application design: retrieval, prompting, tool use, guardrails and fallbacks, drawn as a system with budgets for latency and cost.

llm-econ.text: Inference economics: why generation is slow, where the GPU memory goes, and which lever buys what.

llm-eval.text: Evaluation with no single right answer: building a test set, trusting or distrusting an automated judge, and tying offline scores to online outcomes.

llm-not.text: And judgment about when not to use an LLM at all.

llm-ask.text: Some companies also run coding rounds with an AI assistant allowed, so ask the recruiter about each round.

series.text: This series argues the decisions behind the answers: why a model fails on new data, which loss fits a problem, what serving costs, and how you'd know it broke.

series-count.text: The track's pages ask a hundred and sixty-seven questions. This video answers one. Ten more answer the rest, each once, and a question two pages share is answered once for both.

series-parts.text: First generalization, then the models and how they learn, coding, statistics, deep learning, and NLP. Then system design, and shipping and monitoring models. Last, the two LLM parts: serving them, and evaluating them.

practice.text: Every topic page has concept checks, five challenges run in the browser, and a hundred and ten multiple-choice questions cover the whole track.

next.text: So the first thing an ML round still tests is whether a model works on data it hasn't seen. Next: generalization and evaluation.

llm-not-when.text: It's the question that separates candidates who've shipped from those who've only prototyped. Often a smaller model or a rule does the job better: tabular prediction, a strict latency or cost budget, or a task a regular expression solves.
